meta.title: Materials
meta.subtitle: Folk & Alchemical Reference
meta.description: Metals, gems, plants, and substances historically tied to light or darkness, drawn from folklore, alchemy, and cultural tradition.

items.name: Gold
items.summary: The “king of metals,” tied to the sun across almost every culture that mined it.
items.detail: In Hebrew the word for gold, zahev, literally means “illuminated by the sun.” The Incas called it “the sweat of the Sun.” Plato and Aristotle believed it formed when intense sunlight combined with water underground. Alchemists used a circle-with-a-dot (☉) as the symbol for both the sun and gold, and assigned it Sunday as its day.
items.notes: Masculine metal in most traditions; paired symbolically with the lion for its sun-ray mane.

items.name: Silver
items.summary: Gold’s lunar counterpart — feminine, protective, and tied to night-sky magic.
items.detail: Alchemists called it LVNA, the moon. Selene drove a silver chariot across the night sky in Greek myth, and the Irish god Nuada was given a silver arm with magical properties after losing his own in battle. Long held to ward off evil and bad luck — the folkloric root of the “silver bullet” against werewolves.
items.notes: Sits between light and dark associations: lunar (a night-sky body) but protective against true darkness/evil.

items.name: Iron (“Cold Iron”)
items.origin: Celtic Europe, Rome, near-global apotropaic use
items.summary: The single most widespread ward against fae, ghosts, demons, and witches.
items.detail: Pliny the Elder’s Natural History records iron nails driven into tomb door-lintels to repel nocturnal spirits. Iron scissors were hung over cradles, pins stuck into infants’ clothes, and a piece placed in a birthing bed — all to keep fairies from stealing children. Cemeteries were ringed with iron fences to contain restless ghosts; sickles and horseshoes warded the home generally.
items.notes: Steel (90–98% iron) was treated identically in folk practice. Roughly 1 in 5 fae types (mine spirits, forge spirits) were said to be immune.

items.name: Copper
items.summary: The commoner’s gold — carrying the same solar association for those who couldn’t afford the real thing.
items.detail: Where gold was scarce or unaffordable, copper inherited the same ritual connection to the sun and light. Bronze and brass, copper’s alloys, were correspondingly used as gold-substitutes in ornament and ritual objects throughout the ancient Near East and Bronze Age Europe.
items.notes: Alchemically assigned to Venus rather than the sun, but its ritual “gold-substitute” role persisted in folk practice.

items.name: Lead
items.summary: The alchemical floor — base, heavy, and saturnine; the raw material darkness is transmuted from.
items.detail: Assigned to Saturn, the slowest and most distant of the classical planets, lead was the alchemist’s starting material in the great work of turning “darkness into light” — lead into gold. Its heaviness, dullness, and toxicity made it the natural symbolic opposite of gold’s brilliance.
items.notes: The lead-to-gold transmutation is the most direct metal-based darkness→light ritual concept in Western alchemy.

items.name: Amber
items.summary: Fossilized sunlight — quite literally “drops of the sun” in folk description.
items.detail: Described across cultures as “drops of the sun,” “hardened honey,” and “sunlight solidified.” As fossilized tree resin tens of millions of years old, amber’s golden glow and warmth-to-the-touch made it a natural talisman of captured daylight, often carried as protection or healing charm.
items.notes: Organic, not mineral — grouped with gems by folk tradition rather than geology.

items.name: Moonstone
items.summary: Solidified moonbeams, used for scrying and protection rather than illumination itself.
items.detail: Hindu mythology holds moonstone is made of literal solidified moonbeams. Folklore claims blue moonstones wash ashore every twenty-one years with the tide. By the Middle Ages it was a standard scrying stone for divining the future, and it was carried as a traveler’s protective charm.
items.notes: Lunar light, not solar — culturally distinct from amber’s sun association despite both being “light stones.”

items.name: Obsidian
items.summary: Volcanic black glass, polished into mirrors believed to pierce darkness and reveal hidden truth.
items.detail: Called itzli (“God of Stone”) by the Aztecs, who along with Maya priests fashioned flat sheets of obsidian into scrying mirrors for prophecy. Despite its blackness, folk tradition holds the stone’s sharp edge “pierces into darkness to reveal truth,” and it was carried as a shield against negative or psychic attack.
items.notes: A rare case where a “dark” material is used protectively — darkness fighting darkness, rather than light banishing it.

items.name: Jet
items.origin: Whitby, England; documented in Bald’s Leechbook
items.summary: Fossilized wood, deep black, worn for mourning and carved into wards against witches and lightning.
items.detail: Medieval English texts including Bald’s Leechbook record jet’s amuletic use against lightning, snakebite, and witchcraft. Farmers nailed jet crosses to barn doors; a “witching post” found at Egton carried a jet cross specifically to ward off evil. Jet appears in medieval Christian burials despite the practice running against typical unfurnished burial custom — evidence of genuine magical belief, not mere ornament. Queen Victoria later made it the only acceptable mourning gem at court after Prince Albert’s death.
items.notes: Spanish azabache tradition independently uses jet (often as a fist charm) to protect infants from the evil eye.

items.name: Carbuncle (legendary self-luminous gem)
items.origin: Medieval European bestiary lore; Chilean mining folklore
items.summary: A red gem said to glow with its own inner light, supposedly grown inside a dragon’s skull.
items.detail: Medieval naturalists described precious gems with healing and illuminating power growing inside dragons’ brains — the carbuncle chief among them, glowing red without any external light source. The belief paralleled “toadstones,” curative gems supposedly drawn from living toads’ heads. Chilean folklore separately tells of a small luminous creature, the carbunclo, bearing a glowing gem on its forehead and guarding buried metal.
items.notes: Almost certainly inspired by garnet or ruby; one of the few materials credited with producing light rather than merely symbolizing it.

items.name: Quartz / Rock Crystal
items.origin: Near-global; especially Celtic and Andean traditions
items.summary: Clear stone treated as solidified ice or light, used for scrying and as a sun-focusing tool.
items.detail: Prized for clarity and used to focus or “concentrate” sunlight in folk fire-starting practice, which fed its reputation as a light-holding stone. Andean and Celtic traditions alike used polished quartz spheres for scrying, treating the clear material as a vessel that could hold or transmit vision the way it transmitted light.
items.notes: Functionally similar role to obsidian (scrying) but opposite symbolic valence — clear/light versus black/dark.

items.name: Brimstone (Sulfur)
items.summary: The mineral most associated with hellfire, demonic presence, and the underworld.
items.detail: One of alchemy’s tria prima (with mercury and salt), sulfur represented the combustible “soul” principle. Its yellow color, foul smell, and association with volcanic and hellish landscapes made “fire and brimstone” the standard idiom for divine wrath and the underworld in Judeo-Christian tradition.
items.notes: Symbol 🬍. Despite the “fire” half of the phrase, folklorically grouped with darkness/damnation rather than illumination.

items.name: Rowan
items.summary: The premier protective wood, planted by doorways and carried to repel witchcraft and evil influence.
items.detail: Rowan wood and berries were used throughout the British Isles and Scandinavia as protection against witches and malevolent spirits — branches over doorways, wreaths woven with ivy and bramble at the full moon, walking sticks carried by travelers after dark.
items.notes: Frequently paired with iron in protective charms; the two were considered complementary wards.

items.name: St. John’s Wort
items.summary: Gathered at the summer solstice to “charm all the witches away” and bar misfortune from the home.
items.detail: Its older Latin name, Fuga Daemonum (“flight of demons”), describes its purpose directly. A surviving folk rhyme instructs gathering it at midnight on its Saint’s holy day, then rubbing the door lintels and posts with its red juice to keep thunder, tempest, and harm from the house, with a sprig worn round the neck as a personal charm.
items.notes: Named for St. John the Baptist; gathering coincided with Midsummer Eve, a liminal “witching time” in Frazer’s account of European folk belief.

items.name: Mistletoe
items.summary: Killed the Norse god of light, yet doubles as a ward against witches and werewolves.
items.detail: Balder, the Norse god of light and joy, was the only being mistletoe was never asked to swear an oath of harmlessness to — and so Loki used a mistletoe spear, thrown by the blind god Hodur, to kill him. Despite this, mistletoe (“witch’s broom” in Ozark tradition) was hung in homes and barns specifically to keep witches away, and Virgil’s Aeneid has its “golden bough” grant safe passage through the underworld.
items.notes: Cut traditionally with a golden, non-ferrous blade — iron was thought to spoil its power.

items.name: Mandrake
items.summary: The witch’s root — human-shaped, screaming when pulled, central to flying ointments and necromancy.
items.detail: Its humanoid root shape drove an entire mythology: the screaming-root motif appears across 12th-century Europe and the Middle East simultaneously, and the plant was a named ingredient in flying ointments used for supposed nocturnal witch-flight. Joan of Arc was directly asked at her 1431 interrogation whether she owned a mandrake charm.
items.notes: Most “mandrake” sold historically was actually the also-toxic bryony root, since true mandrake doesn’t grow north of the Mediterranean.

items.name: Deadly Nightshade (Belladonna)
items.summary: The classic witch’s plant — used in flying ointments and listed among the standard “witches’ pharmacopœia.”
items.detail: An 1880s catalogue of witches’ herbs lists belladonna alongside henbane, mandrake, and hemlock “digged in the dark” as the standard tools of folk necromancy, infused into the “hell-broths, philtres, potions, and baleful draughts” of witch legend. Its name (“beautiful lady”) comes from cosmetic use to dilate the pupils.
items.notes: Genuinely toxic and hallucinogenic; the folklore of witch-flight likely stems from its real psychoactive effects.

items.name: Phosphorus
items.summary: Literally named “bringer of light” after its accidental discovery while hunting the Philosopher’s Stone.
items.detail: Searching for gold by distilling vast quantities of human urine, Brand instead isolated a waxy, flammable substance that glowed pale green in darkness. He called it “cold fire.” The name phosphorus comes directly from the Greek for “bringer of light,” and Leibniz himself helped publicize the discovery after touring Europe to see it demonstrated.
items.notes: The first new element discovered in recorded modern history, born from alchemy’s pursuit of transmutation, not light specifically.

items.name: Mercury (Quicksilver)
items.summary: The volatile “spirit” principle of the tria prima — silver-bright, fluid, mediating between states.
items.detail: One of alchemy’s three foundational principles alongside sulfur and salt, mercury represented fusibility and volatility — the spirit that could move between fixed states. Its quicksilver brightness linked it visually to silver and the moon even as its planetary assignment (Mercury) kept it conceptually distinct.
items.notes: Symbol ☿. Neither purely light nor dark in folk tradition; defined by transformation rather than illumination.

items.name: Bonfire Ash
items.summary: The residue of sacred fire, smeared on people and crops for protection after the flames died.
items.detail: On the Isle of Man, communities ensured Beltane bonfire smoke blew over themselves and their cattle; once the fire died down, people smeared its ashes on their bodies and sprinkled them over crops and livestock for protection through the coming season.
items.notes: Ash carried the fire’s protective virtue forward after the light itself was gone — a residue-of-light material.

items.name: Graveyard / Footprint Dirt
items.summary: Earth taken from the place a person stood, thrown after fleeing fairies to break their hold.
items.detail: Folk instruction held that if you encountered fae on Halloween (All Hallows’ Eve), throwing dirt from your own footprint after them would both protect you and force the return of any mortals the fairies had stolen away.
items.notes: An unusual case where ordinary earth, not a refined material, is the active protective substance.

items.name: Salt
items.summary: Placed on the dead to slow decay and symbolically preserve the soul against corruption/darkness.
items.detail: In Irish wake tradition, a plate of salt was placed on the deceased’s chest, believed both to physically slow decomposition and to symbolically preserve the soul. Salt’s purity and incorruptibility made it a natural counter-symbol to decay, darkness, and spiritual corruption across many traditions.
items.notes: Alchemy’s third tria prima principle (with sulfur and mercury) — the fixed, non-combustible “body.”

items.name: Garlic, Bread & Steel (combined charm)
items.summary: A folk trio placed together in cradles, each substance reinforcing the others against fae theft.
items.detail: Documented in 1879 Northumberland folklore: parents placed garlic, bread, and steel together in a baby’s cradle specifically to stop fairies from stealing the child. Garlic itself carries a separate solar association, having been linked to Mars in older herbal tradition.
items.notes: A rare three-material combination charm, rather than a single substance acting alone.

items.name: Turquoise
items.summary: The defining stone of Southwest ritual life — sky, water, and protective power bound into one mineral.
items.detail: The Zuni word for turquoise translates as “sky stone”; the Zuni further split its meaning by color — green turquoise tied to the female and the earth, blue turquoise to the male and the sky — and used a turquoise-and-cornmeal mixture in a ritual cup. The Acoma Pueblo creation account holds that the Creator, Iatiku, taught the people to make turquoise and shell beads carrying real power. The Apache associated it with rain at a rainbow's end and fixed pieces to bows for precision; the Akimel O'odham (Pima) linked it to strength and healing.
items.notes: Despite its sky-blue color suggesting “light,” the Southwest's primary symbolic reading of turquoise is water — the scarcer and more essential resource in an arid landscape.

items.name: Cornmeal
items.summary: A blessing substance scattered to open sacred space and mark the start of the Kachina season.
items.detail: Hopi priests scatter cornmeal across the kiva floor while preparing for the Soyal winter solstice ceremony. During the same rites, the Corn Maiden Kachina marks the openings of the kivas with cornmeal to begin the Kachina season, and corn from every family is gathered and placed on a central altar as a collective prayer for a bountiful year.
items.notes: Functions as a sanctifying/blessing material rather than a light-producing one — its role is to prepare the ritual space where the sun's return is then enacted.

items.name: Pahos (prayer sticks)
items.summary: Feather-and-pinyon offerings crafted to bless homes, animals, and crops ahead of the sun's return.
items.detail: Made by tying feathers and pinyon needles to cut lengths of cotton string, pahos are exchanged among friends and family before the Soyal ceremony, sometimes tied into a recipient's hair, with the giver wishing that “all the Kachinas grant you your wishes.” They are placed in the desert as offerings and used specifically to bless the community's homes, animals, and plants for the coming year.
items.notes: Their creation, not their burning or display, is the ritual act — distinct from candle- or fire-based light materials elsewhere in this list.

items.name: Baltic Amber
items.origin: Baltic coast, Slavic and neighboring trade networks
items.summary: The same fossilized-sunlight resin prized in Western folklore, central to Baltic and Slavic trade and ornament.
items.detail: Baltic amber's trade networks reached deep into Slavic territory for millennia before recorded history, carrying the same “solidified sunlight” symbolic weight documented in broader European folklore. Its warm golden glow made it a natural ornamental and votive material across the region's pre-Christian practice.
items.notes: Shares its core symbolism with the general Amber entry under Gems, but its Baltic source made it a specifically Slavic and Baltic trade commodity rather than a merely imported curiosity.

items.name: Willow & Birch Branches
items.summary: Branches bound with offerings and woven into wreaths as part of seasonal solar ritual.
items.detail: On Kupala Night, willow branches were used to carry strings of offerings exchanged between participants, gathered together and attached as part of the night's ritual structure. Birch was separately favored for the wreaths young women wove from wildflowers and grasses on the day of the festival, later floated on rivers to divine romantic fortune by how they drifted.
items.notes: The wreath itself, not the branch alone, carries the main ritual weight — see the Kupala Wreath ritual entry.

items.name: The Fern Flower (Kwiat Paproci)
items.summary: A legendary flower said to bloom only once a year, at midnight on Kupala Night, granting treasure and hidden knowledge.
items.detail: Ferns do not actually flower, which is precisely the point of the legend: on Kupala Night alone, at the stroke of midnight, a single fiery blossom is said to appear. Whoever finds and picks it gains the ability to see the future, understand animals, and locate hidden treasure — but the search is dangerous, surrounded by demons and spirits who tempt the seeker, and failure to resist their calls while drawing a protective circle around the flower means death.
items.notes: A folkloric material that does not exist in nature — included because the belief in it, and the ritual searches it provoked, are historically real and well documented.

items.name: Perun's Thunderstones (Belemnites)
items.origin: Eastern and Southern Slavic folk belief
items.summary: Fossilized belemnites believed to be the literal arrows or stones hurled to earth by the thunder-and-light god Perun.
items.detail: Across Slavic folk tradition, the bullet-shaped fossils now identified as belemnites were collected and kept as protective talismans, believed to be physical thunderbolts cast down by Perun during his battles against Veles, the serpent god of the underworld and cattle. Houses keeping a thunderstone were thought to be protected from lightning strikes.
items.notes: Connects the Belobog/Chernobog light-versus-dark framework to a tangible, collectible folk object still referenced in regional ethnography.

items.name: The Glowing Skull (Vasilisa's fire)
items.origin: Vasilisa the Beautiful, Russian (Afanasyev collection, 19th c.)
items.summary: A burning skull taken from Baba Yaga's fence, its fire fatal to the cruel and harmless to the deserving.
items.detail: After completing Baba Yaga's impossible household tasks, Vasilisa is given a human skull from the witch's bone fence, its eye sockets burning with fire, mounted on a stick to light her way home. When she arrives, the skull's light flares with sudden brilliance and burns her cruel stepmother and stepsisters to nothing — while leaving Vasilisa completely untouched. She buries the skull in her garden afterward rather than keeping it.
items.notes: A rare fairy-tale material where the same light is simultaneously protective and lethal, depending entirely on the moral character of who stands before it.

items.name: Baba Yaga's Skull Fence
items.summary: A perimeter of human skulls whose eye sockets glow only after full darkness falls, lighting the witch's domain from within night itself.
items.detail: Baba Yaga's hut stands inside a fence built from human bones topped with skulls; by day the fence is inert, but as soon as the “black horseman” (night itself, in the tale's symbolic three-riders structure) passes, the skulls' eyes begin to glow and shine, making the clearing “as bright as midday” despite total darkness having just fallen.
items.notes: Functions as light generated from darkness and death rather than light opposing them — distinct from every other light source in this collection.

items.name: The Cursed Spindle
items.summary: An ordinary spinning tool transformed into the instrument of a century-long magical sleep.
items.detail: In both the Grimm and Perrault versions, a slighted fairy or “wise woman” curses an infant princess to prick her finger on a spindle and die; a final blessing softens the curse into a hundred-year sleep instead. The king's attempt to destroy every spindle in the kingdom fails to prevent the prophecy, and the princess finds the one remaining spindle, hidden in a forgotten tower, on her fifteenth birthday.
items.notes: The thorn hedge that subsequently grows around the castle functions as the tale's darkness-material counterpart — protective and imprisoning at once.

items.name: Stingy Jack's Ember
items.origin: Irish folk tale, basis of the jack-o'-lantern
items.summary: A coal from Hell, placed in a hollowed turnip, that condemns its bearer to wander forever between worlds.
items.detail: Having tricked the Devil twice and barred from Heaven for his sins, Jack is also refused entry to Hell out of the Devil's spite — but is given a single ember from Hell's own fires to light his way through the endless twilight he is condemned to wander. Jack carves out a turnip to hold the coal, creating the original “jack-o'-lantern,” later adapted to pumpkins in North America.
items.notes: One of the clearest folk-tale instances of a light source that is explicitly a punishment rather than a blessing or tool.

items.name: Selenite
items.origin: Contemporary Western crystal practice (no pre-20th-century lapidary basis)
items.summary: Named for the Greek moon goddess Selene; treated in current practice as a self-cleansing source of pure, clarifying light.
items.detail: A soft, water-soluble gypsum, selenite is held in modern crystal work to never require cleansing itself and to actively cleanse other stones placed near it — most commonly paired with black tourmaline, which is left on a selenite plate overnight to be “recharged.” Selenite is associated with the crown chakra and described as elevating the vibration of a space so that “low-level energies cannot exist there,” rather than blocking or absorbing them the way protective stones do.
items.notes: Honest caveat: the idea that selenite cleanses other crystals doesn't appear anywhere in pre-20th-century lapidary literature — it's a genuinely modern (post-1970s) belief, not inherited folklore.

items.name: Citrine
items.origin: Contemporary Western crystal practice; ancient lapidary use as ornament
items.summary: The “sunshine stone” — one of only two crystals modern practice holds never needs cleansing at all.
items.detail: A yellow-to-orange quartz variety colored by trace iron, citrine has been carved as an ornamental gem since roughly 300 BCE in Greece and used for Roman intaglio work. Modern metaphysical practice calls it the “Merchant's Stone,” traditionally tucked into a cash box to attract prosperity, and holds that unlike most crystals it transmutes rather than absorbs negative energy — making it, alongside kyanite, one of the only two stones said to never need cleansing.
items.notes: Genuinely fades to clear or pale quartz under direct sunlight within hours — a real, physically verified property, layered underneath its purely symbolic “sun stone” reputation.

items.name: Black Tourmaline (Schorl)
items.summary: The standard modern “protection” stone — dark, dense, and described as absorbing negativity the way it absorbs light.
items.detail: Black tourmaline is the most commonly recommended protective stone in current Western crystal practice, paired almost universally with selenite in a “protect and cleanse” system: tourmaline absorbs and blocks negative energy, then is placed on selenite to be cleared so it can keep working. Schorl is one of the few minerals exhibiting genuine pyroelectricity and piezoelectricity — real, measurable electrical properties unrelated to its metaphysical reputation.
items.notes: A rare case where a folk material's claimed properties and its actual physical properties are both real, just unconnected to each other.

items.name: Darkness, 15' Radius — Material Component
items.summary: A bit of bat fur plus a drop of pitch or a piece of coal — the canonical arcane material component for Darkness.
items.detail: The 2nd-edition Darkness, 15' Radius spell requires a bit of bat fur and either a drop of pitch or a piece of coal as its material component, producing total, impenetrable darkness that defeats infravision and resists all normal and most magical light. A higher-level drow variant, immobile and centered on the caster, is referenced as existing in supplemental material.
items.notes: Bat fur as a darkness-component ingredient echoes the real-world folk association between bats, night, and the underworld found across many of this list's other entries.

items.name: Dancing Lights — Material Component
items.summary: Phosphorus, wychwood, or a live glowworm — three interchangeable options for the same light-creation spell.
items.detail: The 2nd-edition Dancing Lights spell's material component is specified as “either a bit of phosphorus or wychwood, or a glowworm” — giving casters three folklorically-grounded, naturally-luminous or fire-prone materials to choose between. The spell itself creates up to four torch- or lantern-like lights, glowing orbs resembling will-o'-the-wisps, or a single faintly glowing humanoid shape.
items.notes: Directly mirrors real alchemical history: phosphorus was the literal “bringer of light” substance discovered by Hennig Brand, making this component choice historically grounded rather than arbitrary.

items.name: Light / Continual Light — Spell Mechanics
items.summary: A reversible 1st-level spell: cast normally it produces torchlight; reversed, it produces pitch darkness at half duration.
items.detail: Light creates a torchlight-equivalent glow centered on a chosen point, able to spring from air, rock, metal, wood, or almost any surface; cast directly on a creature's eyes it blinds them (−4 to attack and saves, −4 AC). The spell is explicitly reversible into Darkness using the same casting conditions but at half duration, and multiple castings of Light are non-cumulative — they don't stack to produce brighter light.
items.notes: The single-spell-two-effects reversible structure is a clean mechanical parallel to the real-world Belobog/Chernobog and Selune/Shar dualities elsewhere in this collection.

items.name: Faerie Fire — 2e Mechanics
items.summary: Outlines creatures in a pale glow visible for 80 yards in darkness, granting attackers a bonus against the outlined targets.
items.detail: The 2nd-edition Faerie Fire outlines one or more objects or creatures with pale light, visible at 80 yards in the dark and 40 yards near a bright source; outlined targets become easier to strike, granting opponents +2 to attack rolls in darkness or moonlight and +1 in twilight or better conditions. It can render otherwise-invisible creatures visible once outlined.
items.notes: Mechanically the most combat-relevant light spell in the 2e canon, directly tying illumination to to-hit bonuses rather than pure visibility.

items.name: Shar, Mistress of the Night
items.summary: Greater goddess of darkness, loss, forgetfulness, and the Underdark; malevolent twin of the moon goddess Selune.
items.detail: Shar's portfolio in Faiths & Avatars spans darkness, the night, forgetfulness, and loss, later expanded to caverns, dungeons, and the Underdark after she slew the minor deity Ibrandul. Her clergy is instructed to quench or hide from agents of Selune wherever found, to never plan ahead except under direct clerical oversight, and to treat the dark as “a time to act, not wait.” Her favored weapon, the Disk of Night, is a chakram matching her black-disk holy symbol.
items.notes: Specifically opposed to Lathander (dawn/renewal), Selune (moon), and Shaundakul — the clearest light-versus-darkness deity axis in the Realms' 2e-era pantheon.

items.name: Lathander, the Morninglord
items.summary: Greater god of dawn, birth, renewal, and self-improvement; Shar's direct arch-enemy.
items.detail: Lathander governs dawn, birth, renewal, vitality, and athletics in the core Faerunian pantheon detailed in Faiths & Avatars, framed throughout as the active, optimistic counter-force to Shar's portfolio of loss and stagnation. His faith emphasizes constant self-improvement and new beginnings, themes the setting's lore explicitly maps onto the literal symbolism of each sunrise.
items.notes: Faiths & Avatars devotes roughly equal page-length entries to Lathander and Shar (pp. 90–100 and 138–149 respectively in original pagination), reflecting their structural importance as opposed forces.
